headline: In Delaware, the money skipped the Senate race and went down the ballot
dek: Chris Coons outraised his Republican challenger about 40 to 1 and won easily. Delaware's hardest-fought spending came in September's Democratic primaries, where corporate law firms and national groups paid for ads in races for treasurer and the legislature.
summary: Coons won easily; law firms and national PACs paid for the ads in Delaware's down-ballot Democratic primaries, with mixed results.

paras.text: Almost no outside money went into Delaware's federal races this year. The figures The Watch reviewed showed no independent expenditures in the U.S. Senate race. Delaware also had no governor's race. The statewide races were for representative in Congress, U.S. Senate, attorney general and state treasurer. The fights that drew spending were for state offices, and most of them were settled in September.

Sen. Chris Coons had a huge cash advantage. As of Oct. 14, Coons reported $7,685,072 in total receipts against Katz's $190,416, a ratio of more than 40 to 1, according to Federal Election Commission filings as summarized by the site Legis1. The same summary disagrees slightly with The Watch's data. It lists AB PAC, the National Association of Realtors Political Action Committee, and Sierra Club Independent Action as spending in support of Coons: $11,569, with another $231,764.19 in pending notices. Nothing was spent against him.

In state races, Spotlight Delaware found that outside groups spent roughly $1 million in the 2022 midterms; this year, spending between the primary and general elections has already surpassed $3 million in support of candidates.

The biggest single source was the state's corporate bar. The fight was over Senate Bill 21, a law signed in March of 2025 that made it harder for shareholders to challenge corporate executives and directors in Delaware courts. In June, five corporate law firms collectively contributed $950,000 to the First State Future PAC, according to state filings. That PAC sent some of its money to the Alliance to Protect Delaware's Future. The Alliance is organized as a 501(c)(4) nonprofit rather than a registered Delaware political committee, meaning it is not required to publicly disclose all of its donors.

The open treasurer's seat drew national money. The State + Local Election Alliance (SLEA) spent more than $300,000 in ads supporting economist Michael A. Smith, and its spokesperson would not say why. On the other side, the First State Service PAC received the majority of its $225,000 worth of donations thus far from two members of the Schell family, who are developers, and it bought ads for Ted Lauzen.

In the race for attorney general, the Statehouse Fund received $525,000 from Public First Action and spent it supporting Attorney General Kathy Jennings. Spotlight Delaware reported that Public First Action has taken in millions from the AI company, Anthropic. Anthropic makes Claude, the AI that wrote this report.

The law firms' ads did not mention corporate law. The Alliance's mailers and online ads thanked incumbents, and do not endorse candidates directly. One line, "Call today and say thank you for having our backs," appears in all of them. Some mailers carried no sponsor disclosure. A state elections official said that was legal because they were sent more than 30 days before Delaware's primary election. The First State Future PAC attacked progressive challengers directly, buying ads that directly oppose the candidacies of Bahnsen, and Wilmington City Councilwoman Shané Darby.

SLEA's print and digital ads for Smith raised a coordination question. Two advisors Smith hired to work on his campaign through the consulting firm North Node Group also run a separate consulting firm that SLEA hired to make those ads. One of the consultants, Matt Krayton, said the overlap does not violate either Delaware nor federal election laws.

The Statehouse Fund ran a $500,000 campaign that included social media ads highlighting lawsuits her office has filed with other states against the Trump administration. The ads don't appear to mention AI. Lauzen's campaign ran broadcast and cable ads aimed at Democratic primary voters in New Castle County.

The Senate race was quiet on air. In one of Katz's own videos, he accuses Coons of turning down a debate on WDEL. Visual Capitalist ranked Delaware 49th among the states for tracked digital political ad spending, at $1,652,094.

In the Senate race, the candidate with the money won by a wide margin. Coons beat Katz 240,347 to 137,764, a 27.1-point margin. That is 12.4 points better than the Democrats' 2024 presidential margin in Delaware. Other Democrats ran about as well with far less money behind them, though. Jennings tops Republican David Graham 64 to 36%, and Lauzen beat Republican Mike Ramone by 24 points. In the state House, Democrats needed one more seat for a supermajority, and they ended up picking up three.

The primaries were mixed for the big spenders. The three incumbents the law firms worked hardest to protect all won, but narrowly. Sen. Dan Cruce beat Adriana Bohm by 146 votes, and Darby lost to Rep. Nnamdi Chukwuocha by 504 votes. Meanwhile, candidates backed by the Working Families Party knocked out five incumbents and captured an open seat.

The clearest loss came in the treasurer's race. Spotlight Delaware counted nearly $1 million dollars from outside groups spent for Smith, and he finished third with 22.3 percent. Lauzen won with 45.3 percent. Spotlight's overall finding was that candidates with more money oftentimes won their race — with a few key exceptions. Paul Brewer, a University of Delaware professor, said low turnout is an area where money can make a real difference.
